fixes.explanation: An angel has a nice ring to it, but this passage doesn't mention one in Iconium. Verse 3 says the Lord affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders. So the backup came through what Paul and Barnabas were enabled to do. Friend, I can't add an angel to a text that doesn't have one.

Salamis and Paphos have a great ring to them, but they're not on this map. Verse 6 says they fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region. Those two towns are where the story goes next. I'd have picked a pair by how good the names sound too, friend.
Baal was a false god too, one Israel kept falling for (Judges 2:13). But verse 12 says the crowd in Lystra called Barnabas Zeus. Baal isn't named in this passage.
Dagon was a god the Philistines worshiped (1 Samuel 5:2), so it's a clever pick. But verse 12 says they called Barnabas Zeus. Dagon doesn't appear in Lystra at all. Different crowd, different god.
Builder sounds like a solid job title, friend, but it's not the word here. Verse 12 says they called Paul Hermes because he was the chief speaker. The crowd was reacting to who did the talking.

Yes. Verse 13 says the priest brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, “…hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds.” This was a real plan, with real bulls. Bulls and wreaths at the city gates means somebody was serious.

That's right, friend. Verse 14 says when the apostles Barnabas and Paul found out, “…they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting…” They tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd. That's the text's own picture.
This one is True, friend. Verse 14 says when Barnabas and Paul found out, “…they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting…” They did not sit this one out.

I love stars, my own night sky is full of them. But verse 17 doesn't name them. It says God gives “…rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.” Paul and Barnabas pointed to the rain and the seasons.

A week of rest would sound reasonable to me. But verse 20 says Paul got up and went back into the city, and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. The text has him leaving the next day, not after a week.
Getting driven out would be a rough ending, but verse 21 says something different about Derbe. They preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. No chase scene here.

It would be a safe plan, but they didn't take it. Verse 21 says that after Derbe, they “…returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch…” Those are the same towns where Paul was stoned and where a stoning plan started. They returned to them anyway.

That's what verse 22 says. They were “…strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith.” They came back to those disciples with encouragement. That's good friends right there.

That's the word. Verse 22 says, “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God…” They said it to the disciples they were encouraging. Paul and Barnabas had just lived hard days themselves.

That's right. Verse 23 says they appointed elders in each church, “…praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord, in whom they had believed.” So they prayed and they fasted while they appointed elders. They did it with the Lord in mind.
Caesarea is a good guess, but it isn't named in this passage. Verse 25 says that after Perga, they went down to Attalia. From Attalia they sailed to Antioch.

Asking for a bigger team is how I'd go too, with all these cookie boxes to fill. But the text doesn't say it. Verse 27 says they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them. A report, not a request.
You got it. Verse 27 says God “…had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.” Gentiles means people who weren't Jews. God opened that door, and that's what Paul and Barnabas reported.
Samaritans are a good guess, but they aren't in this report. Verse 27 says God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. That's the word Paul and Barnabas used.
Levites aren't mentioned in this passage. Verse 27 says God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. Gentiles are people who aren't Jews, and that's who the door opened to.
